title: Exploring Soundscape Assessment Methods in Office Environments: A Systematic Review
review_question: Which methods are currently employed to assess soundscapes in office environments? Which factors are typically included in subjective assessments to evaluate the perceived quality of soundscapes in office environments? Which assessment tools are commonly used to evaluate the physical and psychological well-being of office workers in relation to their perception of the sound environment? Which objective acoustic parameters are frequently involved in soundscape assessment in office environments?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies focused on office environments, exploring perceptual aspects of acoustic environments, falling within acoustics/soundscapes/noise studies, involving participants without hearing impairments, and collecting primary data. Excluded studies were those in schools/factories/hospitals, only measuring noise objectively without linking to human perception, focusing on workplace productivity without mentioning acoustics/noise, involving participants with hearing impairments, or being review articles/theoretical papers/using existing databases.

synthesis_conclusions: Both subjective and objective methodologies are widely used for soundscape assessment in office environments.
Questionnaires are the most common subjective tools, often complemented by interviews and discussions.
Direct acoustic measurements and cognitive tasks are frequently employed for objective evaluations.

Subjective acoustic factors include sound source identification, noise disturbance, sound environment perception, acoustic comfort and satisfaction, affective quality of sound environment, office acoustic metrics, and noise control.

Subjective non-acoustic factors include individual characteristics, noise sensitivity, coping strategies, adaptability, cognitive workload, work performance, space dynamics, working habits, and social behaviours.
Questionnaires assessing stress, anxiety, mental fatigue, mood, sleep quality, and burnout are commonly used to investigate the physical and psychological well-being of workers.

Objective acoustic parameters frequently involved are sound pressure level (SPL), Equivalent Continuous Sound Level (LAeq), statistical noise descriptors, reverberation time, speech privacy, and speech intelligibility metrics.
Cognitive tasks are frequently utilized to examine the effects of acoustic conditions on cognitive abilities, including memory, attention, problem-solving, and cognitive flexibility.
evidence_gaps: Refinement is needed to effectively capture the nuances of sound perception in office soundscape questionnaires.
Formalisation and standardisation of soundscape assessment methods for offices are still in early stages, requiring further development.
A unified standard or protocol for soundscape assessment and implementation in office environments is currently lacking.
Future research should focus on refining existing protocols and developing a unified assessment framework adaptable to various settings.
Rigorous validation through pilot studies in diverse real-world environments is needed to ensure the robustness and effectiveness of proposed protocols.
Longitudinal studies are critical for assessing the long-term effects of soundscapes on well-being and productivity, including temporal dynamics and delayed impacts.
limitations: Limiting the search to a single database (Scopus) may have excluded relevant studies, compromising comprehensiveness.
Selection bias may have occurred as initial screening was based solely on titles and abstracts, potentially missing pertinent information.
Data extraction bias could have resulted from subjective interpretation of relevant content by reviewers.
Exclusion of studies inaccessible through UCL Library Services may have affected the completeness and diversity of the data analyzed.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Exploring Soundscape Assessment Methods in Office Environments: A Systematic Review
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The application of the soundscape approach is becoming increasingly prevalent in the evaluation of indoor acoustic environments, including office environments. However, the formalisation and standardisation of soundscape assessment methods for offices remain in the early stages, highlighting the need for further development. This systematic review explores the methods and factors involved in soundscape assessments within office environments, which are intended to contribute to creating or improving comprehensive and widely accepted protocols. This review includes 41 studies, revealing that questionnaires (n = 36) are the most commonly used subjective tools, occasionally supplemented by interviews (n = 1). Some studies employ a combination of questionnaire and interview (n = 2), questionnaire and discussion (n = 1), or all three methods—questionnaire, interview, and discussion (n = 1). Meanwhile, direct acoustic measurements (n = 28) and cognitive tasks (n = 14) are often employed for objective evaluations. Additionally, the review categorises factors involved in objective and subjective soundscape assessments into acoustic and non-acoustic elements. It also identifies tools frequently used to assess the correlation between soundscapes and physical and psychological well-being. Collectively, this review underscores the critical factors for comprehensive soundscape assessments in office environments.

instruments_used.name: Soundscape semantic differential scales
instruments_used.construct: perceived soundscape attributes (e.g., pleasantness, eventfulness, spaciousness)
instruments_used.description: Scales using bipolar adjective pairs to assess subjective soundscape perception.

instruments_used.name: ISO 12913 series questionnaires
instruments_used.construct: soundscape quality, perceived sound sources, soundscape attributes
instruments_used.description: Standardized questionnaires for soundscape assessment, often including questions on perceived sound sources, overall soundscape quality, and specific attributes.

instruments_used.name: Acoustic measurements
instruments_used.description: Measurement of physical sound parameters such as sound pressure levels (e.g., Leq, LAeq), frequency spectra, and background noise levels.

instruments_used.name: Psychoacoustic metrics
instruments_used.construct: perceptual attributes of sound (e.g., loudness, sharpness, roughness)
instruments_used.description: Calculated metrics derived from acoustic measurements that correlate with human perception of sound.

instruments_used.name: Annoyance ratings
instruments_used.description: Direct self-report scales or questions assessing the level of annoyance experienced from sounds.
